analysis.one_liner: Raises fines on insurers and providers that break surprise-medical-billing protections, up to $10,000 per violation.
analysis.headline: A Republican and a Democrat introduced the bill in July 2025, but the Senate health committee has taken no action on it since.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2022 law called the No Surprises Act bans most surprise medical bills — for example, when an out-of-network doctor treats you at an in-network hospital. But the fines for insurers and providers that break those rules are small, and enforcement has been limited. This bill raises the fines to $10,000 per violation, adds a penalty worth three times the unpaid amount when either side slow-walks or dodges payments ordered by the official arbitration process, and requires twice-yearly public reports on audits and enforcement. It was referred to the Senate's health committee in July 2025 and nothing has happened since.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with job-based or individual health insurance who are protected from surprise bills. Stronger fines and mandatory payment deadlines make it more costly for insurers to delay or deny the payments they owe out-of-network providers, and for providers to overcharge, reducing the odds that patients get stuck with illegal balance bills.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured patients facing surprise medical bills

how_it_helps.text: Raises the civil penalty for group health plans and insurers that violate core surprise-billing protections — like sending patients incorrect notices or billing them improperly — from $100 to $10,000 per violation [S2].

Adds a penalty of three times the unpaid amount, plus interest, when a plan or a nonparticipating provider or facility is late or fails to pay after an arbitration determination under the No Surprises Act, including for air ambulance services [S2].
Requires providers and facilities that received more than the arbitration award allows to repay the difference to the plan within 30 days [S2].

Requires federal health agencies to report to Congress every six months on audits, complaints from patients and providers, and enforcement actions, including total fines issued and the most common violations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer health plans that break the surprise-billing rules, and out-of-network providers and facilities — including air ambulance companies — that overbill, delay payments, or keep payments they weren't entitled to. These costs can partly flow through to premiums and provider payment rates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers and out-of-network providers that overbill

drawbacks.text: Heavier fines on insurers and plans raise their costs of doing business, and some of that cost can be passed on through higher premiums or employer benefit costs rather than absorbed by shareholders [S2].

The bill puts real repayment and penalty exposure on out-of-network providers, including small practices, when arbitration awards come in lower than their initial bills — a burden critics of the arbitration process worry can squeeze providers and, over time, narrow the availability of out-of-network care [S2].

The bill adds enforcement mechanics but does not add new funding or staffing for the agencies that would conduct the audits it demands, so tougher penalties on paper may not mean more enforcement in practice [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: surprise medical bills hit hundreds of thousands of insured patients each year, and the existing law's fines are small enough that some plans and providers treat them as a cost of doing business. The costs — some pass-through to premiums and pressure on providers — are real but modest compared with the consumer protection being enforced. The bill's main weakness is that it raises penalties without adding enforcement resources.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2025 and sent to the Senate's Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall introduced the bill on July 23, 2025, with Sen. Michael Bennet as the sole cosponsor, making it a two-person, bipartisan effort [S1][S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; no further action, hearing, or vote appears in the record [S4].
Congress remains in session until January 2027, so the bill could still move, but as of now it has not advanced past its committee referral [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and out-of-network providers that violate surprise-billing rules are better off for now, because the larger penalties have not taken effect and may never.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Plans and providers that overbill, for now

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kansas, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise penalties for violations of the No Surprises Act's balance-billing rules and referred it to the HELP Committee.

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.role: U.S. Senator from Colorado, sole cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it bipartisan from introduction.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Republicans in the 119th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in July 2025 and has taken no action since — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: There is no opposition on the record: the bill has a Republican sponsor and a Democratic cosponsor, and the only obstacle so far is committee inaction rather than a partisan fight.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: The bill raises their penalty exposure from $100 to $10,000 per violation of surprise-billing rules and adds triple-difference penalties for late payments after arbitration. Their interest in avoiding those penalties runs against patients who benefit from enforced billing protections.

industries.industry: Out-of-network hospitals, emergency physicians, and facilities
industries.note: Providers that billed patients or kept payments beyond what arbitration allows must repay within 30 days and face penalties worth three times the unpaid amount for late or skipped payments. The bill targets exactly the overbilling practices that shift costs onto patients.
Air ambulances were among the most frequent sources of surprise bills, and the bill applies the same new payment deadlines and triple-difference penalties to air ambulance arbitration awards.

analysis.trajectory: Most Senate bills die quietly in committee, and this one has sat untouched since July 2025 with a single cosponsor. Barring a push from the HELP Committee leadership or attachment to a larger health package, it is likely to stall for the rest of this Congress.
